title: Statistical mechanics
summary: The microcanonical and canonical ensembles, the classical ideal gas, quantum statistics, Bose and Fermi gases, and phase transitions.
overview: Thermodynamics says what entropy does. Statistical mechanics says what entropy is: the logarithm of the number of microscopic states consistent with a macroscopic description. From that identification the ensembles, the laws of the earlier course, and the properties of ideal gases, quantum and classical, are calculations rather than postulates.

The microcanonical ensemble is counting at fixed energy. The canonical ensemble, at fixed temperature, is the one used for almost every application, and the partition function is its generating object. The classical ideal gas, the equipartition theorem and the Gibbs paradox sit in between. Quantum statistics then distinguishes bosons and fermions, with black-body radiation, electrons in a metal, and Bose–Einstein condensation as the three examples everyone must be able to compute. The last chapter is an introduction to interacting systems and phase transitions, at the level of mean-field theory.
The thermodynamic limit and the difference between a most probable value and a mean value are worth watching. For the systems in this course they agree; the fluctuations tell you by how much.
outcomes: Relate entropy to the number of microstates and derive the thermodynamic identity from the microcanonical ensemble.
Use the canonical partition function to compute free energy, energy, entropy and heat capacity.
Derive the Sackur–Tetrode entropy of a classical ideal gas and resolve the Gibbs paradox.
State the Fermi–Dirac and Bose–Einstein distributions and the assumptions behind them.
Compute the properties of a photon gas, a degenerate Fermi gas and an ideal Bose gas below and above condensation.
Explain a phase transition in mean-field theory, including the Ising model.

history.title: Maxwell’s distribution
history.detail: Maxwell derived the distribution of speeds in a gas at equilibrium from the assumption that the components of velocity are independent.

history.title: Boltzmann’s counting
history.detail: Boltzmann’s paper of 1877 counted the ways of distributing energy among molecules and identified entropy with that count.

history.title: Gibbs’s ensembles
history.detail: Josiah Willard Gibbs’s Elementary Principles in Statistical Mechanics defined the canonical and grand canonical ensembles in essentially their modern form.

history.title: Bose and Einstein
history.detail: Satyendra Nath Bose’s derivation of Planck’s law, extended by Einstein to material particles, began quantum statistics for bosons.

history.title: Fermi–Dirac statistics
history.detail: Fermi and, independently, Dirac applied Pauli’s exclusion principle to a gas and obtained the distribution used for electrons in metals.

history.title: Onsager’s solution
history.detail: Lars Onsager solved the two-dimensional Ising model exactly, showing a phase transition with a logarithmically diverging specific heat.
